title: Particles in a solid, liquid and gas
subject: Chemistry

sources.title: NGSS 5-PS1-1: Develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 1.2 Phases and Classification of Matter

note.text: All matter is made of particles far too small to see. Each dot in this model stands for one particle.

steps.title: Solid
steps.instruction: Dab the particles, packed in neat rows.

note.text: In a solid, particles are packed tightly in a regular pattern. They only jiggle in place, so a solid keeps its shape.
Next, the same kind of model for a liquid, like water in a cup.

steps.title: Surface
steps.instruction: Draw the flat top of the liquid.

note.text: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, with a flat top.

steps.title: Liquid
steps.instruction: Dab the particles, close but jumbled.

note.text: In a liquid, particles are close together but not in rows. They slide past each other, so a liquid can flow.
Last, a gas, like the air in a closed box.

steps.title: Gas
steps.instruction: Dab the particles, spread far apart.

note.text: In a gas, particles are far apart and zoom around. A gas spreads out to fill its whole container.
note.remember: Gas: far apart, fills its container.

steps.title: Label the states
steps.instruction: Pick the right name for each numbered box.

mistakes.Solid: These particles aren't in neat rows, and they have a flat top like water. It's a liquid.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Why does a gas fill its whole container, but a solid keeps its shape?

options.text: Gas particles are far apart and move freely; solid particles are packed in place
options.feedback: Yes. Solid particles only jiggle in place. Gas particles zoom around and spread out to fill the space.
The particles aren't bigger. They're just much farther apart and free to move.
Solids are made of particles too, packed tightly in a regular pattern.
The difference is how the particles are arranged: far apart in a gas, packed in a solid.

steps.title: Invisible matter
steps.question: You can't see air. How can you tell air is made of matter?

options.text: Blowing air into a balloon makes it get bigger
options.feedback: Right. The air particles take up space and push the balloon out, even though each one is too small to see.

options.text: You can't: air is empty space
options.feedback: Air is matter. A balloon fills up because air particles take up space.
Air has no color. But it takes up space, which is why a balloon inflates.
Air is a gas, so it spreads out. It still takes up space, which inflates a balloon.
